result.title: Find my draft short story about the Titanic
result.content_text:
# Find My Draft Short Story About the Titanic

The folder is called *Writing Projects* and it sits on my desktop like it always has. I open it at half past eleven on a Tuesday night, the apartment quiet except for the refrigerator hum and rain against the window. Inside the folder: a screenplay fragment from 2019, three abandoned novel openings, a poem I wrote after my father died that I've never shown anyone, and a subfolder called *Titanic Story, DO NOT DELETE*.

I click it.

Empty.

I sit back. The chair creaks. I try the recycle bin, the search bar, the cloud backup that I pay eight dollars a month for and almost never think about. Nothing. The story is gone. Six thousand words, maybe more, written across four months of early mornings before work. Gone.

I close the laptop and go to bed, but I don't sleep., -

In the morning I call my friend Dara, who is a better writer than me and knows it, but is generous enough not to say so.

"When did you last open it?" she asks.

"March, I think. Maybe February."

"You didn't email it to yourself? Print it?"

"No."

A pause. "That's very you."

She means it kindly. I know what she means. I have a habit of treating my drafts like they're radioactive, keeping them sealed, unshared, as if showing them to anyone would collapse them. The story about the Titanic was the worst of this. I'd told no one it existed. I'd barely admitted it to myself.

"What was it about?" Dara asks.

I look out the window at the street below. A woman walks a small dog. A bus goes past.

"A woman," I say. "Travelling alone. First class."

"Rich?"

"Comfortable. Her husband had just died. She was going back to New York. She'd been in England settling his estate."

"And?"

"And the ship sinks."

Dara laughs, but not unkindly. "Well. That part you can reconstruct.", -

I spend the next three days trying.

I open a new document and type: *April 1912. Southampton.* Then I stare at it. The words look wrong. They look like the beginning of a Wikipedia article, not a story.

The thing about the draft I lost is that it didn't start with the ship. It started with a hat. I remember that clearly. My protagonist, her name was Eleanor, or maybe Ellen, I can't recall which I settled on, was standing in front of a mirror in her cabin, trying to decide whether to wear the black hat or the grey one. She was still in mourning for her husband, technically. The black hat was correct. But she'd worn black for seven months and she was tired of it, and the grey hat had a small blue feather that her husband had never liked, and she thought: *he is dead, and I may wear what I like.*

I write that down. It feels true. It feels like the story.

But the rest won't come., -

What I remember, in pieces:

Eleanor was fifty-one. Not old, but the world of 1912 was prepared to consider her old. She had money enough to be comfortable and not enough to be powerful, which meant she existed in a particular kind of social limbo, invited to the right tables, but never quite at ease there.

She had a daughter in New York, Clara, with whom she had a difficult relationship. Clara was twenty-three and recently married to a man Eleanor didn't trust. The story was, in part, about Eleanor crossing the Atlantic to meet this man properly for the first time, and what she planned to say to Clara, and how the sinking changed those plans, or didn't.

I had a scene in the first-class dining saloon. Long white tablecloths, electric chandeliers, the kind of carved woodwork that takes a craftsman months. Eleanor sitting across from a man whose name I gave as Hartley, not the bandmaster, just a coincidence of names, who was a solicitor from Bristol travelling to meet a client. They talked about nothing important. The food was very good. Eleanor drank a glass of Bordeaux and thought about Clara.

I had a scene on deck, the second day out. Cold, bright, the Atlantic flat and grey-green and enormous. Eleanor walking alone, which was slightly unusual for a woman of her class and noted by other passengers. She didn't care. She'd spent thirty years caring what people noted.

I had the night of the fourteenth., -

That scene I remember most clearly, because I rewrote it four times and was still not satisfied with it when the file disappeared.

Eleanor couldn't sleep. This was not unusual, she hadn't slept well since her husband's death, which was itself not uncomplicated, because she had loved him and also been, for much of the marriage, quietly unhappy, and grief does strange things when it mixes with relief. She put on her dressing gown and sat in the chair by the small porthole and looked at the black water outside.

She felt the ship shudder.

Not a violent thing. More like a held breath, a hesitation. The engines changed their note. She sat forward.

In the corridor outside, nothing. Silence. Then, distantly, footsteps.

She opened the cabin door. A steward was moving quickly down the corridor, not running, but close to it. She asked him what had happened. He told her it was nothing to worry about, ma'am, please return to your cabin. His face said otherwise.

This was the part I rewrote. The first version had Eleanor immediately practical, she dressed, she found her lifebelt, she went to the boat deck. Too efficient. It didn't feel true to a woman who had spent the voyage in a state of suspended feeling, not quite present in her own life.

The second version had her standing in the corridor for a long time, unable to move. Better, but passive.

The third version, I think this is the one I was closest to keeping, had her go back into the cabin and sit down again. Not from paralysis. From a kind of deliberate choice. She thought: *I have been moving toward things my entire life. I have been practical and correct and sensible. I have worn the black hat when I should have worn the grey one.* She sat in the chair and looked at the porthole and thought about Clara, and what she would say when she arrived in New York, and whether she would have the courage to say it.

Then she heard water.

Not much. A sound from below, a gurgling, wrong. And she stood up and dressed and found the lifebelt and went out into the corridor, and this time she moved with purpose, not because she was afraid of dying, but because she had decided she wanted to arrive., -

I can't reconstruct the ending.

I know Eleanor survived. I know she got into a lifeboat, I'd done enough research to know that first-class women had a significantly higher survival rate than third-class passengers of any kind, and I'd wanted to sit with that fact, not resolve it neatly. Eleanor's survival was not heroism. It was class and proximity to the boat deck and a steward who knew which corridors to unlock.

There was a third-class passenger in the lifeboat. A young woman, Irish, travelling alone. I'd given her the name Brigid. In my draft they didn't speak much, I'd resisted the obvious, the cross-class friendship, the meaningful exchange. They sat in the cold and watched the ship go down and didn't speak because there was nothing to say.

But I had written something between them. I can't remember what.

I try several versions. In one, Brigid asks Eleanor where she's going, and Eleanor says New York, and Brigid says she is too, and they leave it at that. In another, Brigid is praying quietly and Eleanor, who has not prayed in twenty years, finds herself listening. In a third, Eleanor gives Brigid her coat, which is warm and good wool, and Brigid takes it without ceremony, and they sit together in the coat's shared warmth until the *Carpathia* comes.

None of these feel like the version I wrote. Or maybe they all do. Maybe I'm misremembering the quality of the original, inflating it because it's gone., -

Dara calls me on Friday.

"How's the reconstruction going?"

"It's not, really. I keep writing around the edges of it."

"Maybe the edges are the story."

I think about this. "What do you mean?"

"You keep telling me what you remember. The hat. The chair. The sound of water. Maybe that's what the story is. Not Eleanor. You."

I don't say anything for a moment.

"That's annoying," I say.

"I know," she says. "Sorry.", -

Here is what I know about why I wrote the story in the first place.

My grandmother was Irish. She came to New York in the 1920s, not on the Titanic, not dramatically, just on a ship, the ordinary kind of passage that millions of people made and that history mostly doesn't record. She worked as a domestic for a family in Brooklyn. She married a man who worked on the docks. She had four children, of whom my mother was the youngest.

She died when I was nine. I remember her hands. I remember that she made bread on Sunday mornings and that the smell of it filled the apartment. I don't remember her voice clearly anymore.

I started thinking about the Titanic after she died, not immediately, years later, because of the third-class passengers. Because of the people in the lower decks who had the farthest to travel to reach the boats and the least time to get there. Because some of them were going to New York for the first time, like my grandmother would later, and they didn't arrive.

I wanted to write about one of them. But I kept writing Eleanor instead. I didn't understand why until Dara said what she said., -

I open the document again. I delete *April 1912. Southampton.* I write:

*My grandmother came to America on a ship. I don't know which one. I never asked her, and then she was gone, and I couldn't ask anyone else because no one else knew either, or if they did they didn't think it mattered. It mattered to me, but I understood too late.*

I read it back. It's not a story. It's a confession.

I keep going.

*I wrote a story about the Titanic because I wanted to give someone like her a name and a face and a coat that kept her warm. I wanted her to survive. I wanted to put her in a lifeboat next to a woman in a grey hat with a blue feather and have them watch the ship go under together and then be taken aboard the Carpathia and wrapped in blankets and given hot tea, and I wanted them both to arrive in New York harbor in the cold April morning and see the city come up out of the water and feel whatever you feel when you have crossed the Atlantic and survived.*

*I lost the draft. I don't know if I can write it again. I'm not sure the story I had was good enough to be worth recovering. But I remember Brigid. I remember Eleanor. I remember the grey hat and the blue feather and the sound of water in the dark.*

*I remember the coat.*, -

I write for three hours without stopping.

It's not the same story. I know that before I've finished the first page. The Eleanor I'm writing now is thinner, less settled in herself, because I'm building her from memory and memory compresses things. The dining saloon scene is shorter. The conversation with Hartley is gone entirely. Some of this is loss. Some of it might be improvement.

Brigid is clearer than she was. I don't know why. Maybe because I've been thinking about her for a week without writing her, and she's had time to become more specific in my mind. She's twenty years old. She's from County Clare. She has a brother already in New York who is supposed to meet her at the pier. She has a cardboard suitcase and a rosary and a letter of introduction to a woman in the Bronx who takes in Irish girls and helps them find work. She has never been on a ship before. She has been seasick for two days and is only just beginning to feel human again.

She does not die. I make sure of that., -

The scene in the lifeboat:

They don't speak for a long time. The water is very cold and very black and the sounds coming from it are not sounds Eleanor will ever be able to describe to Clara, or to anyone. She keeps her eyes on the horizon, or where the horizon should be.

After a while the girl beside her, young, Irish, a thin coat, starts to shiver. Not delicately. Her whole body, uncontrollable.

Eleanor takes off her coat. It is good wool, heavy, warm. She puts it around the girl's shoulders without asking.

The girl looks at her. She doesn't say thank you. Eleanor doesn't want thanks. They sit together under the coat's weight and watch the dark water and wait.

When the *Carpathia* comes, Eleanor helps the girl to the ladder first. Not from nobility. Because the girl is younger and faster and Eleanor is tired and doesn't mind waiting another few minutes. The girl goes up. Eleanor follows.

On deck, someone wraps a blanket around Eleanor's shoulders. Someone gives her tea. She drinks it standing up, looking back at the water, which is empty now and gives nothing back.

She thinks about the letter she will write to Clara. She has been composing it in her head for seven months. She knows now that she will not send a letter. She will arrive in New York and she will go to Clara's apartment and she will knock on the door and when Clara opens it Eleanor will say: *I am here. I want to know your husband. I want to know your life. I have been afraid of this for a long time and I am less afraid now.*

She doesn't know if that's true. But she thinks she can make it true. She thinks that is close enough., -

I save the document. I call it *Titanic Story, Second Draft.*

Then I do something I've never done with a draft before. I email it to Dara.

She replies in twenty minutes: *This is good. The coat is perfect. Keep going.*

I close the laptop. Outside, the rain has stopped. The street is wet and bright under the streetlights. Somewhere below, a door opens and closes, and I hear someone laugh, and then the building is quiet again.

I think about my grandmother's hands. The bread on Sunday mornings.

I think about Brigid climbing the ladder in Eleanor's coat, arriving on the deck of the *Carpathia* in the cold April dark, alive.

I think: *that's enough for tonight.*

I go to sleep.
